title: Exchanges, venues and auctions
objectives: Describe lit exchanges, dark pools and opening and closing auctions.
Find an auction's uncross price as the price that matches the most shares
Choose venues for a large order

screens.prose: At 16:30 the exchange stops continuous trading for this share. For five minutes it only collects orders. Then every matched share trades at **one** price. The table counts who would trade at each price.
screens.question: Tap the price at which the most shares can trade.

hints.text: At each price, the shares traded are limited by the smaller side.
At 503p: 600 buyers but 2,200 sellers, so 600 trade.
Work out the smaller number on every row: 600, 1,000, 1,200, 700, 300.

feedback.correct: At 501p, 1,200 shares trade: more than at any other price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. On each row take the smaller of the two numbers, then pick the largest of those.

byKey.r0: At 503p only 600 buyers will pay, so only 600 shares trade.
byKey.r1: At 502p the 1,000 buyers limit the trade to 1,000 shares. At 501p it is 1,200.
byKey.r3: At 500p only 700 sellers will sell, so only 700 shares trade.
byKey.r4: At 499p only 300 sellers will sell. Most buyers are happy, but there is no one to sell to them.

explain.text: The shares that trade at a price are the smaller of what buyers want and sellers offer. That is 1,200 at 501p, the most on the table. This single price is the **uncross price**, and the event is a closing **auction**.

screens.prose: The same auction as a chart. Green counts buyers willing at each price; orange counts sellers. Slide the price and watch how many shares can trade: the blue dot.
screens.question: As the price rises from 499p to 503p, what limits the shares traded?

options.text: Sellers limit it at low prices and buyers at high prices; the most trade where the two lines cross
Buyers limit it at every price
options.why: At 499p there are 2,500 buyers but only 300 sellers. There, sellers are the limit.

options.text: Sellers limit it at every price
options.why: At 503p there are 2,200 sellers but only 600 buyers. There, buyers are the limit.

options.text: Nothing: the higher the price, the more shares trade
options.why: Higher prices bring sellers but drive buyers away. Above 501p the traded amount falls.

hints.text: At each price, compare the green and orange numbers in the caption.

feedback.correct: The traded amount follows the lower line, so it peaks near the crossing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch which of the two numbers is smaller as you slide.

explain.text: Below 501p sellers are scarce; above it buyers are. The traded amount is the lower of the two lines, so it peaks where they cross, at 501p.

screens.prose: The auction uncrosses at 501p and 1,200 shares trade. Every one of them trades at 501p, even for a buyer whose limit was 503p.
screens.question: How many shares that buyers wanted at 501p or more are left unfilled?

hints.text: How many shares did buyers want at 501p or more, and how many traded?
Buyers wanted 1,500; 1,200 traded.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the shares traded from the buyers at 501p.

byKey.all: 1,500 is what buyers wanted. Only 1,200 could be matched with sellers.
byKey.sell: 1,200 is what traded. The question asks what is left over.
byKey.zero: There are more buyers than sellers at 501p, so some buyers miss out.

explain.text: At 501p buyers want 1,500 and sellers offer 1,200. The 300-share surplus stays unfilled, filled by time priority among the buyers at the margin. The uncross price maximises the matched volume, not the number of happy traders.

screens.prose: A second share's closing auction. The first table lists the orders at each limit. A buy order at 251p will also buy at 250p, and a sell order at 249p will also sell at 250p.
screens.question: Fill in the buyers at or above, and the sellers at or below, each price.

hints.text: Buyers at or above 250p are every buy order with a limit of 250p or more.
Add buy orders down from the top and sell orders up from the bottom.

feedback.correct: Buyers build up as the price falls, sellers as it rises.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add buy orders from the highest limit down, and sell orders from the lowest limit up.

explain.text: Buyers at or above run 500, 800, 1,200, 1,800, 2,000 from 252p down. Sellers at or below run 200, 500, 1,000, 1,400, 2,000 from 248p up.

screens.prose: Here are your totals beside the orders.
screens.question: What is the uncross price, in pence?

hints.text: On each row, take the smaller of the last two columns.
The smaller numbers are 500, 800, 1,000, 500, 200.
The largest of those is 1,000.

feedback.correct: At 250p, 1,000 shares match: the most at any price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the price where the smaller side is largest.

byKey.p251: At 251p only 800 buyers remain, so 800 trade. At 250p it is 1,000.
byKey.p249: At 249p only 500 sellers will sell. At 250p it is 1,000.

explain.text: At 250p buyers want 1,200 and sellers offer 1,000, so 1,000 trade and 200 buy shares miss out. No other price matches more.

screens.prose: A third auction, in a thinly traded share. Only four orders arrive.
screens.question: What is the uncross price?

options.text: There is none: the best buy, 249p, is below the best sell, 251p
250p, halfway between the best buy and the best sell
options.why: You split the gap. A price needs a buyer and a seller who both accept it; at 250p nobody sells.

options.text: 249p, the best buy
options.why: At 249p no seller is willing: the cheapest seller wants 251p.

options.text: 251p, the best sell
options.why: At 251p no buyer is willing: the highest buyer pays 249p.

hints.text: Is there any price where both a buyer and a seller would trade?
Buyers stop at 249p; sellers start at 251p.
At every price one side is empty, so nothing matches.

feedback.correct: No buy limit meets a sell limit, so no shares match and there is no price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a price that both a buyer and a seller accept.

byKey.mid: You split the gap. A price needs both sides; at 250p nobody sells.

explain.text: The book does not overlap: the highest buyer is below the lowest seller. So zero shares match at every price, and the auction has no price. That is the edge case; the orders simply stay in the book.

screens.prose: A **dark pool** shows no book. Orders sit hidden and match at the lit market's mid. The lit book below has a mid of £5.00. You buy 20,000 shares in the dark at that mid instead of at the lit ask.
screens.question: How much do you save on the 20,000 shares, compared with buying at the best lit ask?

hints.text: How far is the mid from the best ask?
Best ask £5.01, mid £5.00: 1p a share.

feedback.correct: 1p a share, the half-spread, on 20,000 shares: £200.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the mid with the best ask, then multiply by the shares.

byKey.full: You saved the whole 2p spread. Buying at the mid saves only the distance from the mid to the ask.
byKey.per-share: That is the saving on one share. You bought 20,000.
byKey.pence: That is the saving in pence. Divide by 100.

explain.text: At the mid you pay half the spread less than at the ask: 1p a share, £200.00 in all. A lit order this size would also walk past the 2,000 shares at £5.01. Hiding size is what dark pools are for.

screens.prose: A colleague says: dark pools are unregulated corners of the market, but they are always cheaper because you trade at the mid. So send every order there.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: A dark fill at mid saves the half-spread, but the order may not fill, and the unfilled part can cost more later
Dark is always cheaper: a mid fill beats the ask every time
options.why: You counted only the shares that fill. Hidden orders often wait unfilled while the price moves away, and you then buy higher.

options.text: Dark pools are unregulated, so prices there are worse
options.why: Dark pools are regulated venues: in the UK and EU they run under MiFID II rules, with caps on dark volume.

options.text: Dark and lit trades cost the same
options.why: A mid fill really does save the half-spread on what fills. The catch is how much fills.

hints.text: What happens to the part of your order that nobody matches in the dark?
A hidden buy at £5.00 fills only if a hidden seller turns up.
If the price rises while you wait, the rest costs more than the lit ask did.

feedback.correct: The saving is real on what fills; the risk is what does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the shares that do not find a match.

byKey.cheaper: You counted only the shares that fill. Unfilled dark orders wait while the price can move against you.
byKey.unreg: You assumed hidden means unregulated. Dark pools are regulated venues with their own rules and volume caps.

explain.text: Dark pools are regulated and save the half-spread when they fill. But there is no pre-trade view, so you cannot see whether a match exists. That is the edge case: a mid fill saves money, a missed fill can cost more.

screens.prose:
The venues you have used:
- **Lit exchange**: a visible book, price-time priority.
- **Dark pool**: hidden orders matched at mid.
- **Auction**: one price, $p^* = \arg\max_p \min\big(D(p), S(p)\big)$.
- **Internaliser**: a firm fills client orders itself, often paying brokers for the flow.

Brokers owe **best execution**; a **smart order router** splits orders across venues to get it.
screens.question: A smart order router gets a buy for 5,000 shares. What does it do?

options.text: Splits it across venues, taking the best prices it can find on each
Sends it all to the main exchange
options.why: You kept to one venue. Best execution means checking where the best price and size are.

options.text: Sends it all to the dark pool to save the spread
options.why: You assumed dark is always best. The router weighs price against the chance of a fill.

options.text: Waits for the closing auction
options.why: Waiting is a choice about time, not routing. The router works with the venues open now.

hints.text: Best execution compares prices across places.
The router splits the order across venues to get the best total result.

feedback.correct: It splits the order across venues for the best overall price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what best execution asks a broker to do.

explain.text: The same share trades on many venues at once. A router reads them all and splits each order to get the best overall fill, which is what best execution requires.

screens.prose: A fund must buy £20m of a FTSE 100 share today. The share trades £200m a day; the chart shows when, in £m, by hour of the day. The closing auction alone trades £50m, the biggest single event of the day.
screens.question: Where should the order go?

options.text: About £15m sliced across the day, lit and dark, and about £5m in the closing auction
One market order for all £20m at 08:00
options.why: One order for £20m walks deep into a thin morning book, as you saw with market impact. It pays far more than the spread.

options.text: All £20m in a dark pool at once
options.why: You trusted one hidden order to fill. It may fill little, and a fund leaves the rest exposed to the price moving.

options.text: All £20m in the closing auction
options.why: £20m is 40% of the auction's £50m. An order that big moves the uncross price against you.

hints.text: Compare £20m with the volume in each part of the day.
£20m is 10% of the day's £200m, but 40% of the closing auction.
Small slices hide in the day's volume, and a modest share of the close fills at one price.

feedback.correct: Slices small against each period's volume, plus a modest share of the close.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep each part of the order small next to the volume it trades into.

explain.text: Each slice stays a small share of the volume it meets, so impact stays low. £5m is 10% of the auction, so it fills at the close without moving the price much. Index funds use the close because it sets the official closing price.

screens.prose: Match each order to the venue that suits it best. Write **L** for a lit exchange, **D** for a dark pool, **A** for the closing auction and **I** for an internaliser.
screens.question: Fill in the venue letter for each order.

rows: Buy 300 shares now at the best visible price
Buy 400,000 shares at mid without showing your size
An index fund buying at the official closing price
A retail app order filled by a wholesaler that pays the broker

hints.text: Which venue shows a visible book, and which hides it?
The official closing price is set by the closing auction.
Immediate small order: lit. Large hidden order: dark. Closing price: auction. Payment for order flow: internaliser.

feedback.correct: Each venue suits a different need: speed, size, the close, or retail flow.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match speed, size, the closing price and payment for order flow to their venues.

explain.text: A small order wanting certainty goes lit. A large order wanting to hide goes dark. A fund tracking the close joins the auction. Retail flow sold to a wholesaler is internalised, under payment for order flow.

ideas: An auction trades every matched share at one price: the one where the smaller of buyers and sellers is largest. No overlap means no price.
Lit books show prices and sizes; dark pools hide them and match at mid, saving the half-spread only on what fills.
Big orders are sliced across venues and the day, and the closing auction is the day's largest liquidity event.

formula.name: Uncross price
formula.note: $D(p)$: buyers at or above $p$; $S(p)$: sellers at or below $p$.

summary.trap: Dark pools are regulated and not always cheaper; the closing price is the auction's uncross price, not the last trade.

quiz.prose: A share's last continuous trade is at 16:29:58 at 502p. The closing auction then uncrosses at 501p for 1.2 million shares.
quiz.question: What is the official closing price?

options.why: You took the last continuous trade. The official close is the auction's uncross price.
You averaged the two. The close is set by the auction alone.

feedback.correct: The closing auction sets the official close.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which event sets the closing price?

explain.text: The closing price is the uncross price of the closing auction, 501p, not the last trade before it. Funds value their holdings at that price, which is why so many trade there.

quiz.prose: Buyers at or above each price: 100p 900, 101p 700, 102p 400. Sellers at or below: 100p 300, 101p 600, 102p 1,000.
quiz.question: What is the uncross price, in pence?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the smaller side at each price, then the largest.

explain.text: The smaller sides are 300 at 100p, 600 at 101p and 400 at 102p. So 600 shares trade at 101p.

quiz.prose: On 6 May 2010 US share prices fell about 9% and mostly recovered within about half an hour, as buyers in the lit books vanished.
quiz.question: What does the flash crash show?

options.text: Displayed liquidity can disappear when market makers pull their quotes
Dark pools caused the fall
options.why: You blamed hidden venues. The fall happened in lit books, as visible bids were withdrawn.

options.text: Auction prices are unreliable
options.why: The crash was in continuous trading, not in an auction.

options.text: Lit books always hold enough depth
options.why: That is what failed: the depth on screen was not there when it was needed.

feedback.correct: A visible book is only as deep as the quotes that stay in it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what happened to the bids.

explain.text: Makers facing toxic, one-way flow widened or pulled their quotes, as adverse selection says they should. With bids gone, sell orders walked down an empty book.

quiz.prose: Lit best bid £12.40, best ask £12.44. A dark pool matches at mid.
quiz.question: At what price does a dark trade happen?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The mid is halfway between the best bid and ask.

byKey.ask: That is the lit ask. Dark pools match at the mid.
byKey.bid: That is the lit bid. Dark pools match at the mid.

explain.text: The mid is $(12.40 + 12.44)/2 = 12.42$. A buyer saves 2p a share against the ask and a seller 2p against the bid.
